INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici curiae comprise a broad range of religious
stakeholders (including nearly 150 individual bishops, conference ministers, clergy, and other faith leaders) who affirm their commitment to peace and human dignity.2  Amici differ in their views regarding a
variety of social issues.  But they  are united in their
belief that reasonable gun regulation is essential to
protect the safety and serenity of places of worship
and the ability of religious institutions to carry out
their missions and activities, all of which are threatened by the alarming  escalation of gun violence in
their communities —including gun violence committed with assault weapons.
Rev. Jihyun Oh, as Stated Clerk of the General
Assembly, is the senior ecclesiastical officer of the
Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)  (PC(USA)), a national
Christian denomination with over 1,000,000 members
in over 8,000 congregations.  The General Assembly is
the highest legislative and interpretive body of the denomination, the final point of decision in all disputes,
and has long held social policy advocating for laws
banning the manufacture, sale and possession of assault weapons.  The General Assembly does not claim
to speak for all Presbyterians, nor are its policies binding on the membership of the Presbyterian Church.

INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Gathering peacefully for prayer and community
is central to the American experience.  Nearly 200
years ago, Alexis de Tocqueville wrote that “Americans of all ages, all conditions, all minds constantly
unite.  Not only do they have commercial and industrial associations in which all take part, but they also

5

have a thousand other kinds: religious, moral, grave,
futile . . . .  [I]f it is a question of bringing to light a
truth or developing a sentiment with the support of a
great example, they associate.”3  For many millions of
Americans, this tendency to join together is expressed
by peacefully gathering for religious observance, a
central aspect of their faith.  Worship communities
are an essential part of this country’s social fabric and
a particular source of its cultural and moral strength.
And yet, in recent years, the peace and tranquility of religious gatherings —precisely the qualities
that make houses of worship safe places for people to
connect, share their faith, and forge community —
have too often been shattered by violent attacks, most
often carried out with firearms.  Some of the most devastating of these attacks have been perpetrated with
AR-15 semiautomatic rifles and similar assault weapons.4  Laws prohibiting these weapons, such as those
enacted in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, provide a measure of protection against the ever-present
threat of gun violence by limiting attackers’ access to
firearms designed to inflict a greater number and severity of injuries than handguns or traditional sporting arms.  Such laws thus reduce the opportunities for
assault weapons to intrude upon the sanctuary of the
worship space.

Exercise of Religious Belief

First Amendment.  See Wisconsin v. Yoder , 406 U.S.
205, 215 (1972) (“The essence of all that has been said
and written on the subject is that only those interests
of the highest order and those not otherwise served

of religion.”).

to worship in peace and without fear.  Houses of worship are intended to provide serene and welcoming
spaces in which members of religious communities
gather together to practice their faith.  The presence
of assault weapons in the community, as well as the
measures needed to protect against them, necessarily
interfere with the serenity of the worship space, creating an environment of fear and unease and chilling
congregants’ right of free exercise:
